Field Notes: How This Works

For parents, staff, and anyone curious what this is

What This Is

A free, no-login science vocabulary review tool for grades 6–8, cross-referenced with national and state science standards. Students pick a grade, then work through this week's new terms or older review terms, at their own pace, on any device — phone, tablet, or school Chromebook.

What This Isn't

Field Notes itself never records a grade or a score, and the site has no login. Most of it is purely for practice and review. There are two places a name and a short response can be submitted, both by opening a short Google Form: the Stay Curious — Entrance Ticket warm-up at the start of each term (ungraded, goes to the teacher's tracking sheet, never scored) and the Weekly Reflection at the end of each new term, which does count toward a grade, submitted through the Form and recorded in the gradebook like any other assignment. Everything above the Weekly Reflection on a term's page stays practice/warm-up only, never scored.

How To Navigate

  • Grade tabs (6 / 7 / 8 / All Grades) — pick a grade level to start. Each tab also shows that grade's episode range (like EP.001–086 for Grade 6) — a personal-tracking number, one per term, running from that grade's first term to its last. It's separate from the podcast's own episode numbers, which follow the actual weekly release order across all three grades combined.
  • ⏮ Last Week's Terms — the previous week's 3 terms, for quick review.
  • 📍 This Week's Terms — this week's 3 new vocabulary terms, matching what's being taught in class right now.
  • ⏭ Next Week's Terms — a look ahead for students who like to work early. The written Journey Guide entry is ready in advance; its optional video/podcast won't be live until that term's own week arrives.
  • 📚 Practice All (Grades 6–8) — every term built across all three grades, regardless of which grade tab is selected. Good for broad review or for a student curious about a sibling's material. Inside this view, terms appear in true episode order for whichever grade or subject filter is selected — first episode to last.
  • 🎯 Practice Grade Only — every term built for just one grade level, in one place.
  • Inside "Practice All," terms can be filtered by subject (Physical / Earth / Life Science) and then by the specific topic within it, for jumping straight to one unit.
  • Each term card walks through eight steps in order: What It Means → Real-World Example → Common Mix-Up → Picture It This Way → Check Your Understanding → Practice (simplify, another example, quiz, compare) → Explore More (video, infographic, podcast) → Faith & Science in Action, with the Weekly Reflection following right after.

🧭 Stay Curious — Entrance Ticket

Opening a term card doesn't dump everything on screen at once. It first shows just a short "Stay Curious" prompt — a quick, optional warm-up question about what the student already knows or is curious about, before any of the actual content appears. Two buttons sit right in that box:

  • ✅ Continue Your Journey — unlocks the full card: all eight steps, Practice, Explore More, Faith & Science, and the Weekly Reflection. A student who doesn't want to engage with the warm-up prompt can tap straight through with zero friction — it's meant to be a brief pause, not a gate that slows anyone down.
  • 📤 Submit Your Response — opens a short Google Form where a student can type their name, grade, and a warm-up response. This is separate from the graded Weekly Reflection journal later on the page — it's a quick, ungraded check-in that goes to the teacher's Field Notes tracking sheet. The small 👁 icon beside it explains where the response goes.

🔭 A Note on "Ask Galileo"

Some terms show an optional "Ask Galileo" button in the Practice section. This is not a chatbot built into the site — clicking it shows a ready-made prompt that a student or parent can copy and paste into whatever AI tool their family already uses (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.). Nothing is sent anywhere by Field Notes itself; the conversation happens entirely in the family's own AI tool, outside this site. The prompt is written to ask guiding questions rather than hand over answers, and it's explicitly instructed never to answer a quiz question directly or draft wording for the Weekly Reflection. It's clearly optional — before using it, please get a parent or guardian's permission and confirm it fits your school's Acceptable Use Policy for technology.

🤖 AI Cohosts

On select terms, a "Meet Your AI Cohosts" button introduces one of several recurring AI-voiced characters (like Quinn Quark or Dr. Cora Cell) who appear periodically in the podcast to help explain a concept in their own voice. They're a fun, consistent presence across episodes — not a chat feature, and not connected to Galileo above.

✝️ A Note on Faith & Science

Every term includes a short Faith & Science in Action reflection, connecting that science concept to Scripture and our Catholic tradition. These reflections aren't meant to be a finished answer — they're meant to open a conversation. We encourage parents and staff to sit with your student for a minute and talk through it together: ask what the connection means to them, whether they see it differently, or where else they've noticed God's hand in the natural world. Science and faith aren't in competition here — both are ways of encountering the same Creator, and some of the richest learning happens in that honest, unhurried conversation, not just in reading a screen alone.

📝 Weekly Reflection

Every term with a Weekly Reflection uses the graded Student Journal: one combined paragraph (at least 75 words) covering the science fact, an example, and an honest answer to that term's Faith & Science in Action question. Scored on Content (0–3) and Grammar & Structure (0–2), for 5 points possible. A bonus point is available for completing it before the end of the school day on the second-to-last day of the school week.

The 📝 Make a Journal Entry button opens a Google Form. A second button, 📖 Review My Journal, is early groundwork for letting a student look back on past entries (with a Download option inside it) — it's a draft preview for now, not yet connected to anywhere entries are actually stored.

Scoring guide for Grammar & Structure, where used:

  • 2 — Clean writing, complete sentences, no distracting errors
  • 1 — Understandable, but has noticeable errors
  • 0 — Errors get in the way of understanding it

A Content score of 1 (as opposed to 0, 2, or 3) isn't a final word — it's a signal that a response showed real effort but stayed shallow, and that student may be asked to revise with more depth before a final score is recorded.

🎧 Listen or Watch Anywhere

Each term gets two different things, not two copies of the same thing: a short video (a quick science demo) and a podcast episode (scripture and personal reflection that goes further than the video does). On YouTube, the short science demos live in one playlist and the full-length podcast episodes live in another — use the "Shorts" or "Full Episodes" link below depending on which you're after. Everything is also being collected into full libraries, so students and parents can watch or listen through the whole set like a regular show — in the car, on a walk, wherever's easiest.

Standards Alignment

Every term is tagged with a Content Statement code from Ohio's Learning Standards for Science (adopted 2018) — the standards Ohio's public and chartered nonpublic schools are required to teach to. Click "📋 See the Standard" on any term to read the actual content statement it supports, straight from that framework.

Why This Matters Beyond This Week

Vocabulary is the foundation science reasoning is built on — a student can't apply a concept they don't yet have language for. Strong term fluency supports how students perform across the standardized science assessments used throughout the year, even though this tool itself is review, not a test-prep program.

It also carries further than this year. Ohio's Learning Standards for Science build their content statements as a K–12 progression (kindergarten through 12th grade), not separate silos per grade. The same standard codes tagged on every term here (like 6.PS.1 or 7.LS.2) continue directly into high school science — a student who walks in already fluent in "atom," "element," or "force" is extending a foundation, not starting from zero.

And because this page is always free, requires no login, and works identically on any device at any hour, it removes the biggest practical barrier to consistent review — the students who benefit most are often the ones without a tutor, a quiet study space, or reliable access at a fixed time.

Updated Weekly

The "New" and "Review" terms rotate every week to match what's being taught in class, so this stays a living companion to instruction rather than a static list.
